extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians writing research papers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, organizing, and presenting mathematical research papers: how to write introductions, state theorems and definitions, organize proofs, prepare abstracts and bibliographies, and decide when/how to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory summary in nontechnical language
rubrics_metrics.description: The first paragraph or two should summarize the main results of the paper in nontechnical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the summary with history of the problem, description of earlier results, and an exact statement of what progress the paper makes; conclude the introduction with acknowledgements and an outline (table-of-contents form or paragraph form). Anti-pattern: opening with technical definitions and technical theorem statements which discourage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain novelty and significance for referee/reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly explain what the paper is about, why you wrote it, why your theorems are new, why the paper makes an interesting contribution, and why its techniques are original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the referee or reader will infer these facts; if the introductory portion is not clear the referee may quickly judge the work as unimportant and reject it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-load exposition, push technicalities to back
rubrics_metrics.description: Place explanatory material (introduction, motivations, context) at the front and technical definitions/statements/proofs later; proceed by gradations from exposition to technical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize so a reader can decide at signposts how far to read; put the hardest technical parts at the end for die-hard readers. This discipline also helps the writer pre-digest and reduce errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize proofs by big steps, defer lemma proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: In the proof section, present the 'big steps' of the proof and show how technical lemmas fit together to yield the theorem; push detailed proofs of lemmas to the end of the paper or later sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid starting a proof section with many technical lemmas that give no indication of direction; instead formulate lemmas where understandable, explain how they combine, and defer nasty details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use signposts in paper and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear signposts so the reader always knows where he/she has been and where he/she is going.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break long proofs into manageable stages; label parts and sections clearly; ensure the status (proved/unproved) of each statement is clear. A reader should at any point know how much effort yields what payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor redundancy to aid readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat definitions, theorems, and reminders when needed rather than assuming once-is-enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a definition or theorem was given many pages earlier and is needed again, give a quick recap or cross-reference so the reader isn't forced to flip back fifty pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theorem statements short and memorable
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to state a theorem in fewer than ten lines, preferably five, ideally a single sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many hypotheses exist, group related assumptions via prior definitions (introduce terms like 'regular', 'amenable', 'smooth') so the main statement is concise and the reader retains the essential structure of hypotheses and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce grouped hypotheses via definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the theorem, define composite terms that bundle several cognate assumptions so the theorem can be stated compactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not sleight-of-hand; it provides organization and context and helps the reader remember the theorem's structure. Always state the definitions formally prior to the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long proofs into lemmas and corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of more than a few pages should be broken into lemmas and corollaries and organized so the reader can follow progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claims and lemmas to isolate technical points; indicate how each piece contributes to the overall argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Claim' to isolate the crux and defer verification
rubrics_metrics.description: State a claim ('We claim that the following is true'), then continue the proof 'Assuming this claim for the moment, we complete the proof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological device tells the reader what the crux is and allows showing the high-level flow before presenting messy verifications; the reader can then choose to study the deferred verification or skip it for now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enunciate technical lemmas at point of use with deferred proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: State a technical lemma right where it is needed and, if its proof would distract, write 'Proof Deferred to Section X.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do this, ensure the paper is well organized, parts are well labeled, and the reader is not left with dangling unproved statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offhand presentation of major results
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not casually announce that you have proved a major theorem in passing without laying out the milestones and honoring the proof steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major results deserve a guided exposition: lay out the extremal problems, normal families, and other milestones; an offhand 'Note that we have proved...' is a disservice to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear phrasing for proofs by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin proofs by contradiction with explicit phrasing like 'Seeking a contradiction, suppose that ...' rather than terse 'Not.' or 'Deny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit phrasing aids communication and avoids cute or cryptic starts that hinder understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: State definitions succinctly and clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should be brief, cogent, and expressed in short simple sentences; build ideas in steps rather than dumping many concepts at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, in textbooks/introductory contexts build stepping stones (function → continuous → intermediate value property) rather than defining everything in one overwhelming paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define only what the audience needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not define standard concepts the expected readership already knows; define new or nonstandard terminology and any notation likely to be misinterpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol/term is standard, refer to a canonical source rather than duplicating; give explicit references (definition number, page, section) to help readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive new terminology or nonstandard notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce more new terminology than necessary; a proliferation of unfamiliar terms may make readers suspect there's nothing substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must introduce new notation, explain its relationship to standard notation and consider whether the new notation is genuinely helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good notation: prefer standard, strive for simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not create new notation when well-known notation exists; if you must, consider several options, consult references, and test on colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good notation can be as important as a theorem (example: notation of differential forms). Strive for clarity and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate definitions preferably as 'if and only if'
rubrics_metrics.description: Technically, definitions should nearly always be in 'if and only if' form; practice often uses 'if' for brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'iff' (Paul Halmos's shorthand) is a modern compromise: brevity plus precision; teaching readers to read definitions is still necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract must be self-contained and concise
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract (usually ≤ ten lines) should convey quickly what the paper is about, be self-contained, avoid bibliographic references, and minimize notation and jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, short, declarative sentences; avoid excessive epsilons-and-deltas — state the type of result and its significance or applications in general terms; consult the target journal's 'Instructions for Authors' and sample abstracts in that journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography: use primary sources and verify details
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble bibliography from primary sources and verify bibliographic data by looking at the actual paper rather than relying on cover/T.O.C. or copied entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid propagating bibliographic inaccuracies; include full information (author, title, journal, volume, year, pages) and, where useful, MR/MathReviews numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only list references that are cited
rubrics_metrics.description: List only references in the bibliography that are cited in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including sentimental or 'might be handy' references; if you include additional helpful works, place them under a separate 'Additional Reading' list and explain their value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give precise pointers in references
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a large work (e.g., a multi-volume text), give specific page/theorem/definition numbers rather than vague 'see X'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps readers follow your path; imprecise citations like 'see Dunford and Schwartz' are inadequate without specific pointers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and use a consistent bibliographic style
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a bibliographic format (acronymic, numeric, Harvard, etc.) and apply it consistently across entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using software like LaTeX/BibTeX or bibliographic databases avoids re-numbering errors and helps maintain consistency; include full details rather than cryptic nicknames only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pros/cons of in-text citations vs end-of-chapter essays
rubrics_metrics.description: In-text citations (acronym/number/author at moment of mention) provide accountability and ensure sources are tied to specific claims; end-of-chapter annotated historical essays (Princeton style) provide broader genesis and context but may overlook minor contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the style that fits the work; in-text citations are customary in most mathematics papers and help retain accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid footnotes for bibliographic references
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, references in footnotes are unusual and often discouraged because footnote tags can be mistaken for exponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most mathematics journals will request reformatting if references are put in footnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use LaTeX/BibTeX and bibliographic databases to manage references
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage LaTeX and BibTeX to assign nicknames, manage numbering, and build bibliographies from a bibliographic database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools save time, avoid renumbering, and allow reuse across papers. Keep a database of references with consistent nicknames; use MathSciNet for MR numbers and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get feedback and gauge reception before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulate preprints, give seminars, discuss results with colleagues to gauge reactions — surprise, confusion, interest — and revise accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider criticisms seriously and make appropriate changes before choosing a target journal for submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn partial results and failures into coherent exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful mathematicians can take partial results, failed attempts, and intermediate calculations and weave them into an attractive tapestry of theorems, corollaries, partial results, and conjectures rather than discarding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not self-promotion; it's the craft of making something of your work and presenting it in publishable form.
